A build, start to finish

Building an electric go-kart

In Year 12, I built one from scratch: welded frame, motor, brakes, wiring, paint, all of it. Here's what actually happened, mistakes included.

6 monthsbuild time
~$300budget, excl. metal
Watch it drive →

Final product — underglow strip and all, mostly because I could.

I'd never welded anything before this. I wanted to actually understand how a vehicle goes together, not just read about it, so I gave myself a budget of about $300 (not counting the metal) and six months to build one from nothing. Plenty of people before me had tried and not finished — usually from running out of time or overcomplicating things. I kept it simple where I could, and fixed what I got wrong.

Steering

Starting out with a mistake

I installed the steering system the wrong way round — steer left and it went right, and vice versa. Had to take it apart and redo the linkage before anything else could move forward.

Motor & drivetrain

Measuring, and making do with what I had

I measured out where the rear axle and motor needed to sit, using mostly secondhand parts to stay on budget. Even the steering wheel was just a rod I bent into shape. A lot of it came down to keeping the mechanisms simple — both for the budget, and because the time constraint mattered more than making anything fancy.

The sprocket had to line up exactly with the motor sprocket and match the axle diameter. I attached it by first fitting something with holes onto the axle itself, so I could screw the sprocket on and adjust it if needed.

Seat & rear axle

Hard rubbish, repurposed

The seat came from hard rubbish — I sawed the legs off, painted it black, and bolted it straight onto the frame. This is also where the rear axle went in, which finally made it a rolling chassis.

Chassis & brakes

Reinforcing it, and getting the brakes to actually work

Once the basic frame worked, I welded on thicker steel to make it safer and stiffer, then wired the brake cable underneath to the front brake and spent a while getting the caliper properly aligned. All the welds on this build were mine — rough at the start, noticeably better by the end.

Electronics

Building somewhere for the wiring to live

Had to enlarge the box later — I hadn't planned for all the electronics it ended up needing: fuse, accelerator control, motor wiring. Also added a cover over the chain so it wouldn't catch anything (or anyone) while driving.

Paint & final assembly

From bare steel to finished kart

A couple of coats of primer, then green for the frame. The sheet metal deck went black, and I wired in the accelerator pedal through the bottom of the deck to the electronics box.

Last touch was underglow strip lighting, plus a proper on/off switch and separate switches for the lights — not strictly necessary, but it's the detail that made it feel finished rather than just functional.

Most of this build was getting something wrong, working out why, and fixing it — the steering, the battery box, the welds all got better the same way. That loop is a big part of why I want to keep doing hands-on, iterative engineering at a bigger scale with Monash Motorsport.
